passage:
Wasim, sixteen, grabbed his scooter keys. The match started in twenty minutes and his helmet was in the cupboard upstairs. "It's only two streets," he said. His cousin Anjali stood on the step with folded arms. "I'm not sitting behind you without one."
His friends at the corner would cheer if he arrived fast and helmetless. Then Wasim remembered the cricket coach's talk last week: the coach had shown the team a helmet split down the middle and said its owner walked away and laughed at the tea stall the same evening. It was a story about a real player in the district.
Wasim sighed, ran upstairs and took the helmet. He arrived three minutes late. His friends laughed. The coach glanced at the helmet and nodded.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the match started?
qa.a: The match started in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when Anjali refused to sit behind him?
qa.a: Wasim felt annoyed and pulled between looking daring and doing the sensible thing.

qa.q: What turning point made Wasim fetch the helmet?
qa.a: He remembered the coach's story of a split helmet and its owner who walked away, and Anjali's refusal to ride without one.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt standing on the step with folded arms?
qa.a: Anjali was probably worried and determined, since Anjali would not ride behind Wasim without a helmet.

grounding: A teenager rides a scooter without a helmet to look daring, and a respected adult's real story shifts the habit.

passage:
Charu leaned into the turn and overtook the auto by inches, keeping up with the boys ahead. Behind her Aadhya gripped her jacket. "Slow down!" Charu laughed and went faster.
At the tea stall afterwards, their swimming coach Nasreen Ma'am sat at the next table. She listened for a minute and put down her cup. "My brother overtook like that when he was your age. The truck driver never saw him. He's alive, but he still cannot lift his left arm above his shoulder."
Charu stopped laughing. Aadhya looked at the table.
On the way home Charu stayed behind the auto for the whole ride. Aadhya loosened her grip a little.

qa.q: Who sat at the next table at the tea stall?
qa.a: Their swimming coach Nasreen Ma'am sat at the next table.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling before the coach spoke?
qa.a: Charu felt daring and pleased with herself, enjoying keeping up with the boys.

qa.q: What turning point changed Charu's riding on the way home?
qa.a: Charu heard the coach's real story about her brother's crash and stopped laughing, then stayed behind the auto for the whole ride.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have felt while gripping Charu's jacket during the overtaking?
qa.a: Aadhya was probably frightened, since she shouted to slow down and loosened her grip only when Charu rode more calmly.

grounding: A teenager overtakes recklessly to look daring, and a respected adult's real story shifts the habit.

passage:
At the junior college in Nashik, Tarun, seventeen, rode his scooter to class every day without a helmet, hair flying, overtaking buses near the gate. His friends cheered. He felt untouchable.
One morning, the vice-principal, Damini Ma'am, stopped him at the gate. She didn't shout. She asked him to come to the assembly hall at lunch.
There, a traffic volunteer, a young man in a wheelchair, spoke to the students. He said he'd been seventeen too, riding without a helmet to impress friends. One wet evening, he skidded. He talked about the months in hospital, and his mother's face.
Tarun couldn't look away.
After the talk, Damini Ma'am said quietly, "I don't want to lose any of you." Tarun stayed back and asked the volunteer where he could buy a good helmet.
The next morning, he wore it. A friend laughed. Tarun shrugged. "Laugh all you want."

qa.q: Who stopped Tarun at the gate?
qa.a: The vice-principal, Damini Ma'am, stopped him at the gate.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling as he listened to the volunteer?
qa.a: Tarun felt shaken and moved, unable to look away from someone who had once felt untouchable like him.

qa.q: What made the difference in changing Tarun's habit?
qa.a: A respected adult who didn't shout and a real story from someone his age were more powerful than peer cheers.

qa.q: How might Tarun's friends see his helmet the next day?
qa.a: Some of his friends may laugh at first, still seeing helmets as uncool.

grounding: A teenager rides without a helmet to look daring, and a respected adult and a real story shift his habit.

passage:
Dear Eshaan Bhaiya,
I saw the video you posted: no helmet, overtaking that truck on the highway, everyone commenting fire emojis. I'm writing because I can't say this on the phone without crying.
You know my friend Ritu from tuition. Last year she was riding pillion without a helmet. Her cousin was showing off. They fell near the flyover. She's okay now, but she spent three months in hospital and still has headaches. Her cousin still can't talk about it.
I know you think nothing will happen to you. Ritu's cousin thought so too.
You're the person I look up to most. Please wear the helmet. Please don't race. If your friends think it's boring, they're not really your friends.
I'll buy you a helmet for Rakhi if that helps.
Your sister,
Vandana

qa.q: How long did Ritu spend in hospital?
qa.a: She spent three months in hospital.

qa.q: How does Vandana feel about Eshaan's video?
qa.a: Vandana feels frightened and upset, unable to talk about it on the phone without crying.

qa.q: Why might Vandana's letter change Eshaan's habit?
qa.a: It tells a real story about someone they know and comes from a sister who looks up to him, which can matter more than friends' approval.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Eshaan might feel shaken and guilty, realising how much his sister worries.

grounding: A teenager writes to her cousin who rides without a helmet and races, using a real story to shift his belief in his own safety.

passage:
Alka, you asked why I'm so strict about helmets now. Okay. When I was sixteen, I thought I was invincible.
I used to ride my brother's scooter to tuition, no helmet, overtaking cars in the gaps, because my friends would clap. One day I tried to squeeze between a bus and an auto. My handle clipped the auto. I skidded. I only scraped my knee, but a truck behind me stopped a foot away.
I remember the driver's face. He got down, very pale, and said, "Beti, I have a daughter your age."
That night my father sat with me. He didn't shout. He told me about his school friend who died riding the same road. I'd never heard that story.
The next day, he bought me a helmet. I still have it. That's why, Alka. I'm Zainab, and I got lucky.

qa.q: What did the truck driver say?
qa.a: He said, "Beti, I have a daughter your age."

qa.q: How did Zainab feel before the accident?
qa.a: Zainab felt invincible and proud, riding recklessly because her friends would clap.

qa.q: What changed Zainab's habit?
qa.a: The near miss, the truck driver's words, and her father calmly sharing a real story about his friend changed her belief in her own safety.

qa.q: How might the truck driver have felt after stopping?
qa.a: The truck driver was probably terrified and shaken, very pale, thinking of his own daughter.

grounding: A young woman recalls riding without a helmet as a teen to look daring, and how a near miss and a respected adult's real story changed her.

passage:
Monday. Lalit rode his brother's scooter to tuition with the helmet hooked on the mirror. "Makes my hair flat," he told Pankaj, who laughed and climbed on behind him, bareheaded too. At the signal Lalit overtook a bus on the wrong side just to hear Pankaj whoop.
Thursday. Their physics teacher, Mr. D'Souza, stopped the lesson and told them about his school friend who skidded on gravel near Mapusa without a helmet and spent months learning to write again. "He was the best bowler in our school," he said quietly. Nobody laughed.
Saturday. Lalit clipped his helmet on before starting the engine and held the spare one out to Pankaj. "Flat hair or no bowling arm. You choose." Pankaj put it on. At the signal, they waited.

qa.q: Where did Lalit keep the helmet on Monday?
qa.a: It was hooked on the mirror.

qa.q: Why did Lalit overtake the bus on the wrong side?
qa.a: Lalit wanted to look daring and enjoyed Pankaj's excitement, feeling sure nothing bad would happen.

qa.q: What shifted Lalit's habit, and why did it work?
qa.a: A respected teacher's real story about a friend's injury made the risk feel real in a way no rule had.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt when Lalit held out the spare helmet?
qa.a: Pankaj was probably a bit surprised but relieved, and happy to follow once his friend made safety the normal thing.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager riding without a helmet and overtaking recklessly to look daring, whose habit shifts after a respected adult's real story.
